intro: Three towers rise 195 meters over Marina Bay, and across their tops floats a 340-meter ship-shaped park with the world's most famous infinity pool. This is how Moshe Safdie turned a casino resort into Singapore's defining silhouette.
page_title: Marina Bay Sands: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: When Singapore decided to build its first integrated resort, it wanted more than a casino. Architect Moshe Safdie answered with a city in the sky: three 55-storey hotel towers holding 2,560 rooms, joined at the top by the Sands SkyPark, a 340-meter platform 200 meters above the street. The whole project cost US$5.7 billion including land, making it the world's most expensive standalone casino property when it opened on 23 June 2010. Safdie called it not just a hotel but a city and a garden.
sections.heading: A ship in the sky

sections.body: The SkyPark is the engineering miracle. It spans all three towers and cantilevers 65 to 67 meters beyond the north tower, one of the largest public cantilevers in the world. Arup's engineers faced a problem with no precedent: three tall towers that expand, contract and sway independently had to carry one rigid platform. The answer was expansion joints at each tower plus tuned mass dampers hidden in the park's belly, working like shock absorbers. The 14 prefabricated steel segments were lifted and joined in mid-air over a 13-week assembly sequence. Up top, 250 trees and 650 plants make it a real tropical garden with room for 3,900 people.
sections.heading: The hardest thing Arup ever built

sections.body: The pool is 150 meters long with a 145-meter vanishing edge, the largest outdoor pool at its height anywhere. It holds 376,500 gallons and was built from 422,000 pounds of stainless steel skinned in 254,000 ceramic tiles. Because the towers move independently, the structural bridges under the pool were built with a three-inch camber so the basin stays level when filled. Two circulation systems run it: one filters and heats the main pool, the other catches the water spilling over the edge and pumps it back. Swimming to the edge looks like a sheer drop, but the water lands in a hidden catchment.
sections.heading: The pool that broke the internet

sections.body: The resort keeps growing around the towers. The lotus-shaped ArtScience Museum opened in the fall of 2010 with immersive exhibitions. Below, the 15,000-square-meter casino atrium hangs a 7-ton chandelier with 132,000 Swarovski crystals, and the Shoppes mall runs a canal through 160,000 square meters of retail where visitors ride sampans between luxury boutiques. The daily Spectra light and water show plays across the bay front. What started as a casino license became Singapore's living room.
sections.heading: The resort around the towers

sections.body:
Crazy Rich Asians (2018) made the SkyPark its finale. Director Jon M. Chu stages the closing engagement party atop the towers, with the infinity pool and the Singapore skyline as the backdrop for Nick and Rachel's last scene. The film, the first Hollywood studio production with an all-Asian cast since Memoirs of a Geisha, turned the already famous pool into a global movie location.

Two years earlier, Independence Day: Resurgence (2016) gave the towers a bleaker cameo. Roland Emmerich's sequel shows Marina Bay Sands' silhouette briefly before the aliens destroy Singapore, one more landmark in the film's world tour of demolition. The appearance is short, but it confirmed the building's status: by 2016 the three towers and their sky-ship were readable worldwide as shorthand for Singapore itself.
